Learning What to Remember: Adaptive Probabilistic Memory Retention for Memory-Efficient Language Models
A Probabilistic Framework for Memory-Constrained Language Modeling

S M Rafiuddin Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Oklahoma State University Affiliation: Stillwater, OK, USA Email: srafiud@okstate.edu    Muntaha Nujat Khan Affiliation: Department of English Affiliation: Oklahoma State University Affiliation: Stillwater, OK, USA Email: munkhan@okstate.edu
Abstract

Transformer attention scales quadratically with sequence length O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}), limiting long-context use. We propose Adaptive Retention, a probabilistic, layer-wise token selection mechanism that learns which representations to keep under a strict global budget MM. Retention is modeled with Bernoulli gates trained via a Hard-Concrete/variational relaxation and enforced with a simple top-MM rule at inference, making the method differentiable and drop-in for standard encoders. Across classification, extractive QA, and long-document summarization, keeping only 3030–50%50\% of tokens preserves ≥95%\geq 95\% of full-model performance while cutting peak memory by ∼35\sim 35–45%45\% and improving throughput by up to ∼1.8×\sim 1.8\times. This architecture-agnostic approach delivers practical long-context efficiency without modifying base attention or task heads.11 1 Accepted at EMNLP 2025 Findings as a short paper.

   

1 Introduction

Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of NLP tasks [1, 2, 3, 4], but their memory requirements grow quadratically with sequence length, posing significant challenges for long-context processing [5]. To address these limitations, various approaches have explored sparse attention patterns to reduce computational and memory overhead [6, 7, 8, 9] and compressed memory representations to extend effective context lengths [10, 11, 20]. Recent work has further proposed dynamic memory and computation strategies, such as internet-scale memory compression [14], token merging for efficient inference [12], and streaming memory management [13]. However, existing methods often either rely on architectural modifications or apply fixed heuristics without explicitly modeling adaptive token retention under strict memory budgets. Inspired by advances in adaptive computation time [16, 17, 18] and improvements in selective attention [19], our approach formulates memory retention as a probabilistic learning problem, enabling language models to dynamically retain the most informative token representations while respecting a global memory constraint. Through this formulation, our approach achieves significant memory savings with minimal performance degradation, offering a flexible and efficient solution applicable to standard transformer architectures.

2 Related Work

Memory-Efficient Self-Attention. The quadratic memory cost of Transformer attention [1] has prompted variants such as Reformer’s locality-sensitive hashing achieving O⁡(L​log⁡L)O(L\log L) [21], Linformer’s low-rank projections for O⁡(L)O(L) [22], and Performer’s random-feature approximations [23]. Sparse patterns appear in Longformer and BigBird [6, 7], and FlashAttention-2 optimizes GPU memory access and parallelism [9].

Memory Compression and External Stores. Compressive Transformer compresses past activations into a secondary memory bank [10], while Memorizing Transformers add an explicit key–value store [11]. Compact summaries are learned in CCM [20], and methods like MEMORY-VQ [14] and GLIMMER [15] apply quantization or late-interaction retrieval.

Token pruning vs. KV-cache compression.

Beyond learned or heuristic encoder-side pruning (e.g., H2O’s fixed heavy-hitter oracle [46]), a parallel line compresses the decoder-side key–value (KV) cache for autoregressive generation, such as SnapKV [47] and PyramidKV [48]. These methods reduce memory/latency during stepwise decoding by selecting or merging past states, whereas our approach targets encoder representations and shrinks the active token set within the stack under a global budget. Consequently, direct apples-to-apples benchmarking is non-trivial: KV-cache compression operates in a causal, decode-time regime with different bottlenecks, while our method improves long-context encoding efficiency without modifying attention patterns. We therefore compare H2O empirically on encoder tasks and discuss SnapKV/PyramidKV qualitatively as complementary techniques for generative inference.

Adaptive Computation and Token Reduction. Adaptive Computation Time (ACT) varies processing steps per token [16], and early-exit models such as DeeBERT and FastBERT skip layers dynamically [17, 18]. Token Merging fuses similar representations [12], and streaming attention sinks manage context retention for low-latency long-sequence processing [13].

Our approach differs by learning probabilistic token retention under a strict global memory budget, enabling end-to-end optimization of which hidden states to store without altering core Transformer architectures.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let 𝐗=(𝐱1,…,𝐱T)\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T}) be the input sequence and let the Transformer encoder produce hidden states 𝐇=(𝐡1,…,𝐡T)\mathbf{H}=(\mathbf{h}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{T}), 𝐡t∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We introduce binary retention indicators 𝐳=(z1,…,zT)∈{0,1}T\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\dots,z_{T})\in\{0,1\}^{T}, defined by

zt={1,if ​𝐡t​ is retained0,otherwisez_{t}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\mathbf{h}_{t}\text{ is retained}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (1)

and denote the masked sequence 𝐇⊙𝐳=(𝐡1​z1,…,𝐡T​zT)\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z}=(\mathbf{h}_{1}z_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{T}z_{T}). Our goal is to learn both model parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} and retention probabilities 𝐩=(p1,…,pT)\mathbf{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{T}), where pt=Pr[zt=1]p_{t}=\Pr[z_{t}=1], by solving

min𝜽,𝐩⁡𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽))]:∑t=1Tpt≤M\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{p}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta})\bigr)\bigr]:\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}\leq M (2)

where MM is the total memory budget (the maximum expected number of retained tokens). At inference, we deterministically retain the top-MM tokens by their retention probabilities {pt}\{p_{t}\}.

Here, ff is the task-specific decoder and ℒ\mathcal{L} the loss; at inference one may further enforce the hard constraint ∑t=1Tzt≤M\sum_{t=1}^{T}z_{t}\leq M.

3.2 Probabilistic Retention Model

We introduce a lightweight summary state 𝐦t∈ℝd\mathbf{m}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and compute context-aware retention probabilities via a gated scoring network:

𝐦t\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{t} =γ​𝐦t−1+(1−γ)​𝐡t,𝐦0=𝟎\displaystyle=\gamma\,\mathbf{m}_{t-1}+(1-\gamma)\,\mathbf{h}_{t},\quad\mathbf{m}_{0}=\mathbf{0} (3)
st\displaystyle s_{t} =𝐯⊤​tanh⁡(𝐖​𝐡t+𝐔​𝐦t−1)+b\displaystyle=\mathbf{v}^{\top}\tanh\bigl(\mathbf{W}\,\mathbf{h}_{t}+\mathbf{U}\,\mathbf{m}_{t-1}\bigr)+b
pt\displaystyle p_{t} =σ⁡(st),zt∼Bernoulli⁡(pt)\displaystyle=\sigma(s_{t}),\quad z_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{t})

where γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] controls the summary decay, σ⁡(x)=(1+e−x)−1\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}, and {𝐖,𝐔,𝐯,b}\{\mathbf{W},\mathbf{U},\mathbf{v},b\} are learned parameters. This formulation captures both local (hth_{t}) and global (mt−1m_{t-1}) context in the retention decision.

3.3 Optimization Objective

To enforce the budget in (2) we introduce a Lagrange multiplier λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and form the saddle-point problem:

maxλ≥0⁡min𝜽,𝐩​ℒλ​(𝜽,𝐩)\max_{\lambda\geq 0}\;\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{p}}\;\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{p}) (4)

where the Lagrangian is defined as

ℒλ​(𝜽,𝐩)=𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽))]+λ⁡(∑t=1Tpt−M)\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{p})&=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta})\bigr)\bigr]\\ &\quad+\lambda\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}-M\Bigr)\end{split} (5)

We optimize by alternating stochastic gradient descent on (𝜽,𝐩)(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{p}) and projected gradient ascent on λ\lambda, i.e. λ←max⁡{0,λ+η⁡(∑tpt−M)}\lambda\leftarrow\max\{0,\;\lambda+\eta(\sum_{t}p_{t}-M)\} at each iteration [24].

3.4 Variational Relaxation

Direct backpropagation through the discrete sampling in (2) is not possible, so we employ the Hard Concrete reparameterization [36, 37].

αt=exp⁡(st),u∼𝒰⁡(0,1)z~t=Clamp[0,1]​(σ⁡(log⁡αt+log⁡u−log⁡(1−u)β)​(ζ−γ)+γ)\begin{split}\alpha_{t}&=\exp(s_{t}),\quad u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)\\ \tilde{z}_{t}&=\mathrm{Clamp}_{[0,1]}\Bigl(\,\sigma\bigl(\tfrac{\log\alpha_{t}+\log u-\log(1-u)}{\beta}\bigr)\,(\zeta-\gamma)+\gamma\Bigr)\end{split} (6)

with temperature β>0\beta>0 and stretch parameters γ<0<1<ζ\gamma<0<1<\zeta. During training we replace ztz_{t} by z~t\tilde{z}_{t} in both the expectation and the Lagrangian ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}, yielding low-variance gradient estimates via the standard reparameterization trick.

3.5 Inference Strategy

At test time we compute retention scores ptp_{t} via (3) and then deterministically select the top-MM tokens by setting

ϕ=the M-th largest of {pt}t=1T,zt∗=𝟏{pt≥ϕ}\phi=\text{the $M$-th largest of }\{p_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T},\quad z_{t}^{*}=\mathbf{1}\{p_{t}\geq\phi\} (7)

so that ∑t=1Tzt∗=M\sum_{t=1}^{T}z_{t}^{*}=M. The encoder outputs are then masked as 𝐇⊙𝐳∗\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z}^{*} and passed to f⁡(⋅,𝜽)f(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}).

4 Experiments

4.1 Datasets & Baselines

Experiments are conducted on six benchmarks: SST-2 (GLUE; short sentences; binary sentiment) [39, 31], IMDb (full movie reviews; avg. 230 words; many > 512 tokens) [32], ArXiv (long scientific papers; avg. 5,000 tokens) [40, 6], QASPER (long-document QA; Exact Match / F1) [33], PubMed (scientific summarization on the RCT subset; ROUGE-1 / ROUGE-L) [41, 34], and CUAD (legal contract clause classification; Micro-F1 / Macro-F1) [35]. Baselines comprise: Full Transformer (dense, no retention), Random Pruning (token masking to meet the budget), H2O (fixed pruning) [46], Constraint-aware Pruning (learned budgeted pruning) [25], Infor-Coef (IB-based dynamic downsampling) [27], and sparse-attention models Longformer (sliding-window) [6] and BigBird (block-sparse with globals) [7]; we also report zero-shot LLM references GPT-3.5 [28], Llama 2 [29], Llama 3 [30], Falcon [42], Mistral [43], Gemma [44], and Phi4-Mini [45]. Our method is Adaptive Retention. DistilBERT-base-uncased (≈\approx66M) for SST-2/IMDb/CUAD and Longformer-base-4096 (≈\approx149M) for ArXiv/QASPER/PubMed.

4.2 Experimental Setup

We fine-tune DistilBERT-base-uncased on the short-context benchmarks, SST-2, IMDb, and CUAD, and Longformer-base-4096 on the long-document benchmarks, ArXiv, QASPER, and PubMed RCT, under token-retention budgets M/T∈{0.5,0.3}M/T\in\{0.5,0.3\}, comparing against the baselines described above. We optimize with AdamW (lr=3×10−5\mathrm{lr}=3\times 10^{-5}; weight​_​decay=0.01\mathrm{weight\_decay}=0.01), training for three epochs on SST-2/IMDb/CUAD (batch size 32) and one epoch on ArXiv/QASPER/PubMed RCT (batch size 16). Hard Concrete relaxation uses β=0.66\beta=0.66, γ=−0.1\gamma=-0.1, ζ=1.1\zeta=1.1, and the Lagrange multiplier λ\lambda is updated via projected ascent (step size η=1×10−2\eta=1\times 10^{-2}).

4.3 Main Results

Extended analysis.

Tables 1 and 2 (six benchmarks; three seeds, mean) show that Adaptive Retention (AR) preserves task accuracy while operating under strict 50%/30% token budgets and remains competitive with both pruning baselines and sparse-attention models.

Against dense (no retention). On SST-2, Adaptive Retention is within 0.6 pp at 50% (91.5 vs. 92.1) and within 1.6 pp at 30% (89.2 vs. 90.8). On IMDb, it attains 94.1/92.3 vs. 94.8/93.6; on ArXiv (R1) 80.9/79.5 vs. 81.3/80.1. For QASPER, Adaptive Retention matches dense F1 at both budgets (65.0 / 63.0) with EM just 0.2 pp lower (43.8 / 39.8 vs. 44.0 / 40.0). On CUAD, Adaptive Retention stays within 0.2–0.5 pp of dense (micro/macro), and on PubMed RCT it trails by 2.0 pp on ROUGE-1 at each budget while matching ROUGE-L. These gaps are small relative to the 50–70% token savings.

Against heuristic pruning (H2O, Random). Adaptive Retention consistently outperforms H2O and Random across tasks and budgets. At 50%: vs. H2O, Adaptive Retention is +2.5/+2.6/+2.4 pp on SST-2/IMDb/ArXiv; on QASPER it is +5.3 EM and +4.5 F1 (43.8/65.0 vs. 38.5/60.5); on PubMed RCT +2.0 (R1) and +2.5 (RL); on CUAD +3.8 (micro) and +3.8 (macro). At 30%: Adaptive Retention beats H2O by +3.7/+3.4/+3.9 pp on SST-2/IMDb/ArXiv; on QASPER by +3.3 EM/+4.5 F1; on PubMed RCT by +2.0 R1/+2.5 RL; and on CUAD by +4.0 micro/+3.8 macro. Relative to Random, gains are larger (e.g., +6.5 pp on SST-2 and +7.2 pp on IMDb at 30%).

Against sparse-attention (Longformer, BigBird). On ArXiv, Adaptive Retention slightly exceeds both baselines at both budgets (80.9/79.5 vs. 80.1/78.0 and 80.7/79.1). On the remaining tasks, gaps are small—typically ≤1\leq 1 pp and occasionally up to 2 pp (e.g., PubMed RL and QASPER F1 at 50%)—indicating that learning which tokens to keep can close most of the gap to architectures that change how attention is computed.

Zero-shot LLM references. Prompted GPT-3.5, Llama 2/3, Mistral, Gemma, and Phi4-Mini trail fine-tuned encoder baselines on these supervised evaluations, especially for long documents and budgeted settings, underscoring that general-purpose zero-shot models are not directly comparable under the same retention constraints.

Ablations, throughput, and memory. Table 3 shows accuracy/efficiency degrade when core pieces are removed. Without variational relaxation (no Hard–Concrete), SST-2/IMDb/ArXiv drop 1.3/1.4/1.9 pp at 50% (1.4/1.8/2.7 pp at 30%), and 30% throughput falls from 1.80×1.80\times to 1.60×1.60\times (7.5 GB→\to7.2 GB). Disabling alternating optimization hurts by 0.7/0.9 pp, 1.0/1.1 pp, and 1.4/2.3 pp; fixing the Lagrange multiplier costs 0.5/0.5 pp, 0.5/0.5 pp, and 1.1/1.6 pp, with smaller gains (1.701.70–1.75×1.75\times, 7.3–7.4 GB). Threshold pruning trails by 2.4–3.9 pp and only reaches 1.40×1.40\times/7.1 GB. In contrast, full Adaptive Retention stays near dense accuracy while delivering the best throughput (1.80×1.80\times at 30%) and strong memory savings (7.5 GB); see Fig. 2 for stable hyperparameter regions.

Budget choice (30% vs. 50%). Moving from 50%→\to30% typically yields an additional ∼\sim20–25% latency reduction and ∼\sim0.4–0.8×\times extra throughput, with accuracy drops of ∼\sim1–2 pp on short-text classification and ∼\sim0.6–1.0 pp on long-document tasks. Practitioners targeting strict memory/latency caps can favor 30%, while 50% offers a near-lossless regime for accuracy-sensitive deployments.

5 Conclusion

Adaptive Retention learns which tokens to keep via Bernoulli gating with Hard–Concrete relaxation and a Lagrangian budget, closely matching full-sequence accuracy while reducing memory and latency. Ablations validate each component (Table 3), and the method drops in to standard Transformers across context lengths.

Limitations

We highlight four main limitations. (i) No evaluation on autoregressive decoding. Our study targets encoder-style tasks only. Extending Adaptive Retention to decoding would require a dynamic KV cache: (a) causal caching that stores hidden states only for retained tokens; (b) amortized updates that score the newly generated token each step and maintain a top-MM cache via a small priority queue (min-heap) replacement; and (c) bounded attention over this fixed-size memory bank to cap compute/memory regardless of sequence length. We leave the empirical validation of this design to future work. (ii) Overhead profile. The retention scorer adds O⁡(T)O(T) work (linear in sequence length) but is lightweight in practice (<2%<\!2\% latency in our profiles); most gains come from operating on progressively smaller token sets in deeper blocks and downstream heads while leaving the base attention mechanism unchanged. (iii) Scale. Results are on medium-scale backbones (e.g., DistilBERT, Longformer-base); behavior at billion-parameter scales remains to be demonstrated. (iv) Hyperparameters. Performance shows some sensitivity to the budget penalty and relaxation controls (e.g., β,γ,ζ\beta,\gamma,\zeta); however, we observe robustness plateaus and provide default settings and sweeps in the appendix to guide new deployments.

Appendix A: Compute Cost Breakdown

As Table 4 shows, under a 30 % token-retention budget our Adaptive Retention method processes a batch in just 0.27 s, nearly twice as fast as the Full Transformer’s 0.48 s, translating to a 1.80× throughput gain and reducing per-1 000-token time from 0.96 s to 0.54 s. Longformer and BigBird also improve over the dense baseline (1.55× and 1.45×, respectively), but Adaptive Retention achieves the highest speed-up with the least memory overhead. At a 50 % budget these differences shrink (e.g. our method’s per-batch time would rise toward ∼\sim0.35 s), so focusing on 30 % clearly illustrates the peak efficiency benefits of learned retention.

Appendix B: Layer-wise Token Retention Analysis

A comparison of Tables 5 and 6 shows consistent depth-wise decay, but the absolute values labeled “30% Budget” exceed the stated per-layer budget: DistilBERT declines from 45.2 % to 38.5 % and Longformer from 50.0 % to 34.0 %. Because the method defines per-layer retention as keeping the top Ml=⌊ρ​Tl⌋M_{l}=\lfloor\rho T_{l}\rfloor tokens with ρ∈{0.5,0.3}\rho\in\{0.5,0.3\}, these Appendix B percentages (≈34​–​50%\approx 34\text{--}50\,\%) are inconsistent with a 30 % target and should be corrected or explicitly explained. Under the “50% Budget,” per-layer retention increases (e.g., DistilBERT 47.1%→52.3%47.1\,\%\to 52.3\,\%, Longformer 38%→60%38\,\%\to 60\,\%) while preserving the same decay profile, and the total drop remains larger across 12 layers (≈16\approx 16 pp) than across 6 layers (≈6.7\approx 6.7 pp); interpret these trends only after reconciling the budget definition.

Appendix C: Slackness Guarantee

Proposition 1.

Let

F∗=min𝜽,𝐩∑t=1Tpt≤M⁡𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽))]F^{*}=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{\theta},\,\mathbf{p}\\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}\leq M\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}))\bigr] (8)

Let (𝛉λ,𝐩λ)(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda},\mathbf{p}_{\lambda}) be any minimizer of the Lagrangian

ℒλ​(𝜽,𝐩)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{p}) =𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta})\bigr)\bigr] (9)
+λ⁡(∑t=1Tpt−M)\displaystyle\quad+\;\lambda\Bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}-M\Bigr) (10)

and define the slack

Δ=∑t=1Tpt,λ−M.\Delta\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t,\lambda}-M. (11)

Then the following slackness bound holds:

Δ≤F∗−𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩λ)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽λ))]λ\Delta\;\leq\;\frac{F^{*}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p}_{\lambda})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda}))\bigr]}{\lambda} (12)
Proof.

By definition of F∗F^{*}, there exists a feasible (𝜽∗,𝐩∗)(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*},\mathbf{p}^{*}) with ∑tpt∗≤M\sum_{t}p^{*}_{t}\leq M achieving

𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩∗)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽∗))]=F∗\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p}^{*})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}))\bigr]=F^{*} (13)

Since ∑tpt∗≤M\sum_{t}p^{*}_{t}\leq M, the Lagrangian satisfies

ℒλ​(𝜽∗,𝐩∗)=F∗+λ⁡(∑tpt∗−M)≤F∗.\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*},\mathbf{p}^{*})=F^{*}+\lambda\bigl(\sum_{t}p^{*}_{t}-M\bigr)\leq F^{*}. (14)

Optimality of (𝜽λ,𝐩λ)(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda},\mathbf{p}_{\lambda}) implies

ℒλ​(𝜽λ,𝐩λ)≤ℒλ​(𝜽∗,𝐩∗)≤F∗\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda},\mathbf{p}_{\lambda})\;\leq\;\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*},\mathbf{p}^{*})\;\leq\;F^{*} (15)

Expanding ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda} at (𝜽λ,𝐩λ)(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda},\mathbf{p}_{\lambda}) gives

ℒλ​(𝜽λ,𝐩λ)=𝔼𝐳∼Bernoulli⁡(𝐩λ)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐇⊙𝐳,𝜽λ))]+λ​Δ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda},\mathbf{p}_{\lambda})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbf{p}_{\lambda})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{H}\odot\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda}))\bigr]+\lambda\,\Delta (16)

Combining the above,

𝔼⁡[ℒ]⏟Lλ0+λ​Δ=ℒλ​(𝜽λ,𝐩λ)≤F∗,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}]}_{L_{\lambda}^{0}}\;+\;\lambda\,\Delta=\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\lambda},\mathbf{p}_{\lambda})\;\leq\;F^{*}, (17)

so rearranging yields

λ​Δ≤F∗−Lλ0⟹Δ≤F∗−Lλ0λ,\lambda\,\Delta\leq F^{*}-L_{\lambda}^{0}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Delta\leq\frac{F^{*}-L_{\lambda}^{0}}{\lambda}, (18)

as claimed. ∎

Appendix D: Unbiasedness of the Hard-Concrete Estimator

Lemma 1 (Unbiased Gradient Estimator).

Under the Hard-Concrete relaxation, define

z~=g⁡(u,p),u∼U⁡(0,1)\tilde{z}=g(u;p),\quad u\sim U(0,1) (19)

so that z~∼Bernoulli⁡(p)\tilde{z}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). Then

g^​(p)=∇pℒ​(f⁡(H⊙z~,θ))\hat{g}(p)=\nabla_{p}\,\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot\tilde{z};\theta)\bigr) (20)

satisfies

𝔼u∼U⁡(0,1)​[g^​(p)]=∇p𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θ))]\mathbb{E}_{u\sim U(0,1)}[\hat{g}(p)]=\nabla_{p}\,\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(H\odot z;\theta))\bigr] (21)
Proof.

Since z~=g⁡(u,p)\tilde{z}=g(u;p) has the same law as z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p), we have

∇p𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θ))]=∇p𝔼u∼U⁡(0,1)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙g⁡(u,p),θ))].\nabla_{p}\,\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)}\!\left[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot z;\theta)\bigr)\right]=\nabla_{p}\,\mathbb{E}_{u\sim U(0,1)}\!\left[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot g(u;p);\theta)\bigr)\right]. (22)
∇p𝔼u​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙g⁡(u,p),θ))]=𝔼u​[∇pℒ​(f⁡(H⊙g⁡(u,p),θ))].\nabla_{p}\,\mathbb{E}_{u}\!\left[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot g(u;p);\theta)\bigr)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{u}\!\left[\nabla_{p}\,\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot g(u;p);\theta)\bigr)\right]. (23)

and the right-hand side is exactly 𝔼u​[g^​(p)]\mathbb{E}_{u}[\hat{g}(p)]. Thus the estimator is unbiased. ∎

Appendix E: Variance Bound on Gradient Estimates

Lemma 2 (Variance Bound).

Suppose the loss ℒ\mathcal{L} is LL-Lipschitz in its input activations, and let

g^​(p,ui)=∇pℒ​(f⁡(H⊙g⁡(ui,p),θ))\hat{g}(p;u_{i})\;=\;\nabla_{p}\,\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\!\odot\!g(u_{i};p);\theta)\bigr) (24)

be the per-sample gradient under the Hard-Concrete reparameterization g⁡(u,p)g(u;p), with ui∼U⁡(0,1)u_{i}\sim U(0,1) i.i.d. Form the Monte Carlo average over BB samples:

g¯B​(p)=1B​∑i=1Bg^​(p,ui)\bar{g}_{B}(p)\;=\;\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\hat{g}(p;u_{i}) (25)

Then there exists a constant CC (depending on LL, γ\gamma, and ζ\zeta) such that

Var⁡[g¯B​(p)]≤CB\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\bar{g}_{B}(p)\bigr]\;\leq\;\frac{C}{B} (26)
Proof.

Since the uiu_{i} are independent,

Var⁡[g¯B​(p)]=1B2​∑i=1BVar⁡[g^​(p,ui)]=1B​Var​[g^​(p,u)].\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\bar{g}_{B}(p)\bigr]=\frac{1}{B^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\hat{g}(p;u_{i})\bigr]=\frac{1}{B}\,\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\hat{g}(p;u)\bigr]. (27)

It remains to bound Var​[g^​(p,u)]\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}(p;u)]. By the Lipschitz assumption,

‖g^​(p,u)‖\displaystyle\bigl\|\hat{g}(p;u)\bigr\| =‖∇pℒ​(f⁡(H⊙g⁡(u,p),θ))‖\displaystyle=\bigl\|\nabla_{p}\,\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot g(u;p);\theta)\bigr)\bigr\| (28)
≤L​‖∂pf⁡(H⊙g⁡(u,p),θ)‖\displaystyle\leq L\,\bigl\|\partial_{p}f(H\odot g(u;p);\theta)\bigr\|
≤L​C0\displaystyle\leq L\,C_{0}

for some finite C0C_{0} that depends on the stretch parameters γ,ζ\gamma,\zeta and the network Jacobian. Therefore

Var⁡[g^​(p,u)]≤𝔼⁡[‖g^​(p,u)‖2]≤(L​C0)2=:C\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\hat{g}(p;u)\bigr]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\hat{g}(p;u)\|^{2}\bigr]\;\leq\;(L\,C_{0})^{2}=:C (29)

Combining,

Var⁡[g¯B​(p)]≤CB\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\bar{g}_{B}(p)\bigr]\;\leq\;\frac{C}{B} (30)

as claimed. ∎

Appendix F: Convergence of the Alternating SGD–Ascent Scheme

Proposition 2 (Two-Timescale Convergence).

Assume the following:

  1. 1.

    The function ℒλ​(θ,p)=𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θ))]+λ⁡(∑tpt−M)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta,p)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)}[\mathcal{L}(f(H\odot z;\theta))]+\lambda(\sum_{t}p_{t}-M) has continuously differentiable gradients in θ,p\theta,p, and these gradients are Lipschitz continuous.

  2. 2.

    The step-sizes {αk},{βk},{γk}\{\alpha_{k}\},\{\beta_{k}\},\{\gamma_{k}\} for updating θ,p,λ\theta,p,\lambda satisfy the Robbins–Monro conditions:

    ∑k=1∞αk\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{k} =∑k=1∞βk=∑k=1∞γk=∞,\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\beta_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_{k}=\infty, (31)
    ∑k=1∞αk2,∑k=1∞βk2,∑k=1∞γk2\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{k}^{2},\;\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\beta_{k}^{2},\;\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_{k}^{2} <∞\displaystyle<\infty

    and the timescales are separated: αk=o⁡(βk)\alpha_{k}=o(\beta_{k}) and βk=o⁡(γk)\beta_{k}=o(\gamma_{k}).

Then the stochastic updates

θk+1\displaystyle\theta_{k+1} =θk−αk​∇θℒλk​(θk,pk)+ξkθ\displaystyle=\theta_{k}\;-\;\alpha_{k}\,\nabla_{\theta}\,\mathcal{L}_{\lambda_{k}}(\theta_{k},p_{k})+\;\xi_{k}^{\theta} (32)
pk+1\displaystyle p_{k+1} =Proj[0,1]T​{pk−βk​∇pℒλk​(θk,pk)+ξkp}\displaystyle=\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]^{T}}\bigl\{p_{k}\;-\;\beta_{k}\,\nabla_{p}\,\mathcal{L}_{\lambda_{k}}(\theta_{k},p_{k})+\;\xi_{k}^{p}\bigr\}
λk+1\displaystyle\lambda_{k+1} =[λk+γk​(∑t=1Tpk,t−M)]+\displaystyle=\bigl[\lambda_{k}\;+\;\gamma_{k}\bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{k,t}-M\bigr)\bigr]_{+}

(where ξkθ,ξkp\xi_{k}^{\theta},\xi_{k}^{p} are zero-mean martingale noises and [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} denotes projection onto λ≥0\lambda\geq 0) converge almost surely to a stationary point (θ∗,p∗,λ∗)(\theta^{*},p^{*},\lambda^{*}) of the saddle-point objective minθ,p⁡maxλ≥0​ℒλ​(θ,p)\min_{\theta,p}\max_{\lambda\geq 0}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta,p).

Proof Sketch.

This result follows by casting the updates as a two-timescale stochastic approximation (SA) algorithm (cf. Borkar & Meyn, 2000). On the fastest timescale (αk\alpha_{k}), the θ\theta-iterate tracks the gradient descent on ℒλk​(⋅,pk)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda_{k}}(\cdot,p_{k}) treating (pk,λk)(p_{k},\lambda_{k}) as quasi-static. On the intermediate timescale (βk\beta_{k}), the pp-iterate tracks descent on ℒλk​(θk,⋅)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda_{k}}(\theta_{k},\cdot) treating λk\lambda_{k} as static but θk\theta_{k} as nearly equilibrated. Finally, on the slowest timescale (γk\gamma_{k}), λ\lambda ascends the dual coordinate ∑tpt−M\sum_{t}p_{t}-M.

By standard SA theory:

  • •

    Each iterate sees the slower variables as frozen, satisfying the single-timescale convergence conditions under Lipschitz gradients and Robbins–Monro step-sizes.

  • •

    The timescale separation αk≪βk≪γk\alpha_{k}\ll\beta_{k}\ll\gamma_{k} ensures that the coupled process tracks the solutions of its limiting ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in each block.

  • •

    The projected ascent on λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 preserves boundedness and feasibility of the dual variable.

Consequently, the joint process converges almost surely to an internally chain-transitive invariant set of the limiting ODE, which under mild convexity/concavity assumptions reduces to the set of saddle points of ℒλ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}. Hence (θk,pk,λk)→(θ∗,p∗,λ∗)(\theta_{k},p_{k},\lambda_{k})\to(\theta^{*},p^{*},\lambda^{*}), concluding the proof. ∎

Appendix G: Duality-Gap & Slackness Trade-off

Lemma 3 (Duality Gap Bounds Slackness).

Let

F∗=minθ,p∑tpt≤M⁡𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θ))]F^{*}\;=\;\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\theta,p\\ \sum_{t}p_{t}\leq M\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(H\odot z;\theta))\bigr] (33)

and let (θλ,pλ)(\theta_{\lambda},p_{\lambda}) be any (possibly infeasible) minimizer of the Lagrangian

ℒλ​(θ,p)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta,p) =𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θ))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)}\Bigl[\mathcal{L}\bigl(f(H\odot z;\theta)\bigr)\Bigr]
+λ⁡(∑t=1Tpt−M)\displaystyle\quad+\lambda\Biggl(\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}-M\Biggr) (34)

Define the budget slack

Δ=∑tpt,λ−M\Delta=\sum_{t}p_{t,\lambda}-M (35)

and the duality gap

Gapλ=ℒλ​(θλ,pλ)−F∗\mathrm{Gap}_{\lambda}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda},p_{\lambda})\;-\;F^{*} (36)

Then the following bound holds:

Gapλ≥λ​Δ⟹Δ≤Gapλλ\mathrm{Gap}_{\lambda}\;\geq\;\lambda\,\Delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Delta\;\leq\;\frac{\mathrm{Gap}_{\lambda}}{\lambda} (37)
Proof.

By definition of F∗F^{*}, any feasible (θ,p)(\theta,p) with ∑tpt≤M\sum_{t}p_{t}\leq M satisfies

𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θ))]≥F∗\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(H\odot z;\theta))\bigr]\;\geq\;F^{*} (38)

Hence for the particular (θλ,pλ)(\theta_{\lambda},p_{\lambda}),

𝔼z∼Bernoulli⁡(pλ)​[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θλ))]≥F∗\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{\lambda})}\bigl[\mathcal{L}(f(H\odot z;\theta_{\lambda}))\bigr]\;\geq\;F^{*} (39)

Now expand the Lagrangian at (θλ,pλ)(\theta_{\lambda},p_{\lambda}):

ℒλ​(θλ,pλ)=𝔼⁡[ℒ⁡(f⁡(H⊙z,θλ))]⏟g​e​F∗+λ​Δ≥F∗+λ​Δ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda},p_{\lambda})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(f(H\odot z;\theta_{\lambda}))]}_{\\ geF^{*}}\;+\;\lambda\,\Delta\;\geq\;F^{*}+\lambda\,\Delta (40)

Rearranging gives

ℒλ​(θλ,pλ)−F∗≥λ​Δ\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda},p_{\lambda})-F^{*}\;\geq\;\lambda\,\Delta (41)

i.e. Gapλ≥λ​Δ\mathrm{Gap}_{\lambda}\geq\lambda\,\Delta. Dividing by λ>0\lambda>0 yields the desired slackness bound. ∎

Appendix H: Generalization Bound under Random Token Retention

Theorem 1.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a class of predictors ff mapping token sequences of length TT to ℝ\mathbb{R}, and suppose the loss ℓ⁡(f⁡(x),y)\ell(f(x),y) is bounded in [0,1][0,1]. Denote by ℜ^n​(ℱ)\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{F}) the empirical Rademacher complexity of ℱ\mathcal{F} on nn full-length examples. Now introduce a random retention mask z∈{0,1}Tz\in\{0,1\}^{T} that selects exactly MM positions uniformly at random, and define the masked predictor f~​(x,z)=f​(x⊙z)\tilde{f}(x,z)=f(x\odot z). Then the Rademacher complexity of the masked class satisfies

ℜ^n({(x,y)↦ℓ(f~(x,z),y)})≤MTℜ^n(ℱ).\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}\bigl(\{\,(x,y)\mapsto\ell(\tilde{f}(x,z),y)\}\bigr)\;\leq\;\frac{M}{T}\;\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{F}). (42)

As a consequence, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the choice of an i.i.d. sample and masks,

∀f∈ℱ:𝔼[ℓ(f(x⊙z),y)]\displaystyle\forall\,f\in\mathcal{F}:\quad\mathbb{E}\bigl[\ell(f(x\odot z),y)\bigr] ≤1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(f⁡(xi⊙zi),yi)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\bigl(f(x_{i}\odot z_{i}),y_{i}\bigr) (43)
+2​MT​ℜ^n​(ℱ)\displaystyle+2\,\frac{M}{T}\,\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{F})
+3​ln⁡(2/δ)2​n\displaystyle+3\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}\,

so the generalization gap increases by at most O⁡(M/T)O(M/T) relative to the full-sequence bound.

Proof.

Let {σi}i=1n\{\sigma_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} be Rademacher variables. By definition,

ℜ^n​({ℓ∘f~})=1n​𝔼σ​supf∈ℱ∑i=1nσi​ℓ​(f⁡(xi⊙zi),yi).\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}\bigl(\{\ell\circ\tilde{f}\}\bigr)=\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\,\ell\bigl(f(x_{i}\odot z_{i}),y_{i}\bigr). (44)

Since ℓ\ell is [0,1][0,1]-valued and Lipschitz in its first argument, Talagrand’s contraction lemma implies

ℜ^n​({ℓ∘f~})≤1n​𝔼σ​supf∈ℱ∑i=1nσi​f​(xi⊙zi)\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}\bigl(\{\ell\circ\tilde{f}\}\bigr)\leq\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\,f(x_{i}\odot z_{i}) (45)

Condition on the masks {zi}\{z_{i}\}. Each term σi​f​(xi⊙zi)\sigma_{i}\,f(x_{i}\odot z_{i}) involves only the MM retained positions, so its Rademacher complexity is reduced by a factor M/TM/T:

𝔼z​[supf∈ℱ∑i=1nσi​f​(xi⊙zi)]≤MT​𝔼σ​supf∈ℱ∑i=1nσi​f​(xi)\mathbb{E}_{z}\Bigl[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\,f(x_{i}\odot z_{i})\Bigr]\;\leq\;\frac{M}{T}\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\,f(x_{i}) (46)

Dividing by nn gives ℜ^n​({ℓ∘f~})≤MT​ℜ^n​(ℱ)\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\{\ell\circ\tilde{f}\})\leq\frac{M}{T}\,\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{F})

The high-probability generalization bound for Rademacher complexity (see, e.g., [38]) then yields the stated inequality, completing the proof. ∎

Appendix I: Complexity Reduction Guarantee

Proposition 3 (Complexity Reduction Guarantee).

Assume a Transformer-style layer where each token retained incurs 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) memory (for its key, query, and value vectors). Then:

  • (i)

    In full dense attention over TT tokens, storing the T×TT\times T attention matrix costs

    𝒪⁡(T2​d)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}\,d) (47)

    memory.

  • (ii)

    Under learned retention of exactly MM tokens, only the M×MM\times M submatrix among retained tokens need be stored, costing

    𝒪⁡(M2​d)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}\,d) (48)

    memory.

  • (iii)

    Computing the attention scores in a mixed full–sparse regime (where each of the TT tokens attends only to the MM retained tokens) requires

    𝒪⁡(T​M​d)\mathcal{O}(T\,M\,d) (49)

    time per layer.

Proof.

  1. (i)

    In standard full attention, one forms the T×TT\times T matrix of pairwise dot-products. Each of the T2T^{2} entries is an inner product of dd-dimensional vectors, i.e. 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d). Hence total memory and time are both 𝒪⁡(T2​d)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}\,d).

  2. (ii)

    With learned retention, let S⊆{1,…,T}S\subseteq\{1,\dots,T\} be the MM retained indices. Only the |S|×|S|=M2|S|\times|S|=M^{2} block of attention weights among retained tokens is stored (plus negligible overhead for mapping), yielding 𝒪⁡(M2​d)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}\,d) memory.

  3. (iii)

    For a mixed scheme where every token (retained or pruned) still queries the retained set SS, one computes TT query–key products of size dd each against only MM keys. Thus total work per layer is T⋅MT\cdot M products of cost 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d), i.e. 𝒪⁡(T​M​d)\mathcal{O}(T\,M\,d).

∎
